problem.math: F : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R},\quad \text{find } x \in \mathbb{R}^d \text{ such that } F(x) \text{ is as small as possible}
problem.description: Stochastic optimization with access to sample losses f(\cdot,\xi) whose expectation is F.

definitions.description: The paper denotes the error in d_t by epsilon_t; it measures the error incurred by using d_t instead of the unknown direction \nabla F(x_t).

assumptions.name: independent_samples
assumptions.math: \text{We assume access to a stream of independent random variables } \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_T \in \Xi

assumptions.name: function_oracle
assumptions.math: \text{for all } t \text{ and for all } x,\quad \mathbb{E}[f(x, \xi_t)|x] = F(x)

assumptions.name: differentiable_losses
assumptions.math: \text{We assume that } f(x, \xi_t) \text{ is differentiable, and } L\text{-smooth as a function of } x \text{ with probability } 1.

assumptions.name: L_smooth_losses
assumptions.math: \text{Define a differentiable function } f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} \text{ to be } L\text{-smooth iff } \|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\| \leq L\|x-y\| \text{ for all } x \text{ and } y. \text{ We assume that } f(x, \xi_t) \text{ is differentiable, and } L\text{-smooth as a function of } x \text{ with probability } 1.

assumptions.name: G_lipschitz_losses
assumptions.math: \text{Define a differentiable function } f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} \text{ to be } G\text{-Lipschitz iff } \|\nabla f(x)\| \leq G \text{ for all } x. \text{ We will also assume that } f(x, \xi_t) \text{ is } G\text{-Lipschitz for our adaptive analysis.}

assumptions.name: Theorem1_parameter_choice
assumptions.math: b > 0,\quad k = bG^{2/3}/L,\quad c = 28L^2 + G^2/(7Lk^3) = L^2(28 + 1/(7b^3)),\quad w = \max\left((4Lk)^3, 2G^2, \left(ck/(4L)\right)^3\right)

initialization.name: algorithm_initialization
initialization.math: \text{Input: Parameters } k,w,c, \text{ initial point } x_1;\quad \text{Sample } \xi_1;\quad G_1 \leftarrow \|\nabla f(x_1,\xi_1)\|;\quad d_1 \leftarrow \nabla f(x_1,\xi_1);\quad \eta_0 \leftarrow \frac{k}{w^{1/3}}

output.math: \text{Choose } \hat{x} \text{ uniformly at random from } x_1, \ldots, x_T. \text{ (In practice, set } \hat{x} = x_T\text{). return } \hat{x}

main_theorem.statement_math: \text{Under the assumptions in Section 3, for any } b > 0, \text{ we write } k = bG^{2/3}/L. \text{ Set } c = 28L^2 + G^2/(7Lk^3) = L^2(28 + 1/(7b^3)) \text{ and } w = \max\left((4Lk)^3, 2G^2, \left(ck/(4L)\right)^3\right) = G^2\max\left((4b)^3, 2, (28b + 1/(7b^2))^3/64\right). \text{ Then, Storm satisfies }\quad \mathbb{E}[\|\nabla F(\hat{x})\|] = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \|\nabla F(x_t)\|\right] \leq \frac{w^{1/6}\sqrt{2M} + 2M^{3/4}}{\sqrt{T}} + \frac{2\sigma^{1/3}}{T^{1/3}},\quad \text{where } M = \frac{8}{k}(F(x_1)-F^*) + \frac{w^{1/3}\sigma^2}{4L^2k^2} + \frac{k^2c^2}{2L^2}\ln(T+2).
main_theorem.rate: Noiseless rate O(ln(T)/sqrt(T)); stochastic term O(sigma^{1/3}/T^{1/3}).
main_theorem.measure: Expected norm of the gradient at a uniformly random iterate, equivalently the expected average of gradient norms over x_1,...,x_T.

proof.description: Introduce the Lyapunov potential and derive the two parameter side conditions used throughout the proof.
Apply Lemma 2 with index shifted from t to t+1 to bound the change in the weighted error term.
proof.produces: First displayed upper bound for the weighted error increment.

proof.description: Use a_{t+1}\leq 1 to simplify the error increment bound and label the three displayed contributions A_t, B_t, and C_t.
For A_t, substitute the adaptive stepsize and compare the denominator with the shifted cumulative gradient norm sum.
proof.produces: The summand for A_t is put into the form required by Lemma 4.

proof.description: Apply Lemma 4 to the shifted A_t sum and use the G-Lipschitz bound to obtain the logarithmic estimate.
Expand B_t and substitute a_{t+1}=c\eta_t^2, isolating the reciprocal stepsize difference and the coefficient 4L^2-c.
Use concavity of x^{1/3} to start bounding \eta_t^{-1}-\eta_{t-1}^{-1}.
Use w\geq 2G^2 and then G_t\leq G to continue the reciprocal stepsize estimate.
Use \eta_t\leq 1/(4L) to finish the reciprocal stepsize difference estimate.
Use the theorem's definition of c to bound the coefficient \eta_t(4L^2-c).
Combine the reciprocal stepsize estimate with the coefficient bound to obtain the negative B_t bound.
Put together the A_t bound, B_t bound, and the C_t contribution to get equation (4).
Use Lemma 1 and the Lyapunov definition to bound one-step potential change.
Sum the one-step potential bound and substitute equation (4) so the error terms cancel.
Reorder the summed potential inequality to bound the weighted gradient norm sum by the initial/final potentials and logarithmic term.
Use the lower bound F^* and nonnegativity of the error term in \Phi_{T+1} to replace potentials by F(x_1)-F^* and the initial error.
Use d_1=\nabla f(x_1,\xi_1), \eta_0=k/w^{1/3}, and the gradient noise bound to control the initial error.
Derive the proof's monotonicity fact: since the adaptive denominator w+\sum_{i=1}^tG_i^2 is nondecreasing, \eta_t is decreasing.
Use the decreasing stepsizes to lower bound the weighted gradient sum by \eta_T times the unweighted squared-gradient sum.
Apply Cauchy-Schwarz with A = sqrt(eta_T sum ||grad||^2) and B = 1/sqrt(eta_T).
Define M as in the proof and combine the weighted gradient bound with Cauchy-Schwarz up to the displayed kM/\eta_T term.
Use the adaptive stepsize identity for \eta_T to replace kM/\eta_T by the cumulative sampled-gradient expression.

Define the noise variable \zeta_t and split each sampled gradient norm into deterministic gradient and noise parts; because \xi_t is independent of the past algorithm history, the fixed-x gradient-noise assumption applies at the random iterate x_t.
proof.produces: \zeta_t := \nabla f(x_t,\xi_t)-\nabla F(x_t), with conditional_noise_bound_at_random_iterate: \mathbb{E}\|\zeta_t\|^2\leq\sigma^2 after conditioning on the past history that determines x_t.

proof.description: Plug the G_t split into the root-sum bound and use (a+b)^{1/3}\leq a^{1/3}+b^{1/3} to separate noise and deterministic-gradient contributions.
Use the variance bound on \zeta_t and concavity to replace the noise contribution by M(w+2T\sigma^2)^{1/3}, while leaving the deterministic-gradient expectation as printed.
Use concavity of x \mapsto x^a for a\leq 1 on the deterministic-gradient term to move expectation inside the exponent.
Set X to the square root of the squared-gradient sum and rewrite the preceding estimate as a scalar inequality.
Record the paper's two alternatives implied by the scalar inequality.
Solve the first alternative for \mathbb{E}[X]; the proof's final displayed bound uses the larger earlier quantity w+2T\sigma^2.
Solve the second alternative by dividing by (\mathbb{E}[X])^{2/3} and raising to the 3/4 power.
Combine the solved cases to obtain the paper's displayed bound for \mathbb{E}[X].
Use Cauchy-Schwarz to pass from the root of the squared-gradient sum to the average gradient norm, then split (w+2T\sigma^2)^{1/6}.
proof.produces: Theorem 1 bound for the uniformly random output.

Use \eta_t\leq 1/(4L) to collect coefficients and subtract F(x_t) from both sides.
